row_review_ledger.claim_adjudication: The interaction itself is well established (also by crystal and cryo-EM structures of MlaA-OmpF/OmpC, PMID:29038444, PMID:38092770), but bare protein binding carries no functional information. The biologically meaningful content (MlaA acting with porins in outer-membrane phospholipid removal) is captured by the cell outer membrane, intermembrane phospholipid transfer and the contributes_to phospholipid transfer activity core function. No more specific porin-binding molecular function term exists that would add information. Removal follows the protein binding policy and does not question the reported interaction.

As for the OmpF row: the OmpC-MlaA complex is real and functionally important (removing OmpC phenocopies mlaA loss in stationary phase), but generic protein binding is uninformative. The function of the complex is represented by the process and core-function annotations. Removal does not dispute the interaction.

Co-purification of MlaA with OmpF is a genuine physical association, but generic protein binding conveys no function. The informative content of this paper for MlaA (an MlaA-OmpF complex that MlaC docks onto for lipid exchange) is captured by the intermembrane phospholipid transfer process and the contributes_to phospholipid transfer activity core function.

Correct and appropriately specific. The outer-membrane location is supported experimentally (porin association that is sufficient to target non-lipidated MlaA to the OM; crystal structure placing MlaA in the inner leaflet of the OM).

The computational prediction (SPaseII lipoprotein signal peptide, lipidated Cys18) agrees with experimental localization of MlaA to the outer membrane, so the annotation is correct and consistent with the IEA row for the same term.
MlaA is specifically an outer-membrane protein, already annotated to GO:0009279 cell outer membrane (ACCEPT above); the informative descendant should replace the generic membrane term.

MlaA performs the outer-membrane lipid extraction/loading step, supported by structures, native perturbations and purified OmpF–MlaA-dependent MlaC loading (PMID:40168124). This supports participation in intermembrane phospholipid transfer. The term is direction-neutral; that does not imply equal experimental support for competing net directions.

Consistent with the IBA row and with later structural and biochemical work showing MlaA-to-MlaC phospholipid transfer at the outer membrane (PMID:38092770). Only the abstract is cached, but the abstract itself states the role of the OmpC-MlaA complex in the Mla pathway, and the curator-assigned process is clearly correct for MlaA.

The interaction is well established, but bare protein binding is uninformative under the protein-binding policy. Its functional consequence, stabilization of MlaF and its assembly into MlaFEDB, is captured by the NEW protein stabilization annotation and the complex membership term (GO:0043190). Removal does not dispute the interaction.
Bare protein binding is uninformative; the MlaF contact is a subunit interaction within MlaFEDB, represented by complex membership (GO:0043190) and the protein stabilization process.

Cytoplasm is correct but broader than the supported cytosolic pool and cytoplasmic surface of the inner membrane. The soluble STAS subunit binds MlaF at that face in the assembled transporter; refine to cytosol and extrinsic component of cytoplasmic side of plasma membrane. This does not make MlaB an integral membrane protein.
Abstract-only cache, so the specific observation cannot be checked, but a soluble cytoplasmic location is consistent with all structural data for MlaB; defer to the curator.
MlaB is not named in the cached main text (presumably in the supplementary protein lists), but cytosolic detection agrees with MlaB being a soluble cytoplasmic protein; defer to the curator.

The full PMID:20128927 study documents stress-survival phenotypes and yrbB complementation in E. coli K-12 derivatives. GO:0006974 denotes a cellular response to DNA damage, not only DNA repair, so an envelope function does not refute it. These experiments do not resolve whether MlaB performs a damage-triggered response or its constitutive envelope role changes survival. Retain that mechanistic uncertainty without dismissing the IMP observation or inferring a PAINT loss.

Correct but general; the specific supported process is intermembrane phospholipid transfer (GO:0120010), which MlaB already carries by IBA and IDA.

MlaB is not itself a membrane protein, but as a stoichiometric MlaFEDB subunit bound to MlaF it sits at the cytoplasmic face of the inner membrane, so GO:0031234 extrinsic component of cytoplasmic side of plasma membrane is the accurate refinement. PMID:29358647 has no mention of Mla proteins in its full text and does not support the row.

Verified in the full text; the antibiotic lethality phenotype is the primary screen readout and was complemented, so the acts_upstream_of_or_within annotation is supported. It is an indirect consequence of envelope homeostasis defects, not a core MlaB function.

MlaB contributes structurally to the transporter by stabilizing MlaF and enabling MlaFB assembly with MlaED; mlaB mutants have the Mla lipid-asymmetry phenotype. The gammaproteobacterial MlaB node placement is appropriate.

Abstract-only cache, but the abstract describes the reconstituted transport system containing MlaFEDB; consistent with the full-text evidence that MlaB is required for MlaFEDB assembly and activity. Defer to the curator for assay details.

GO:0120014 requires phospholipid removal from a membrane or particle, protection in a hydrophobic pocket during aqueous transport, and delivery to an acceptor membrane or particle. MlaB stabilizes and regulates the MlaF-containing complex; it is not the lipid-bearing aqueous shuttle. The reconstituted MlaFEDB/MlaC assay supports a contribution to this collective activity, retained in core_functions, rather than assigning the entire carrier activity to this individual subunit. This is a function-scope judgment, not a general rule that complex subunits must work in isolation.

Complex membership is correct, but GO:1990531 is defined as "A protein complex that functions as a phospholipid-translocating P-Type ATPase" (synonyms P4-ATPase complex, DRS2-CDC50 complex) and is not classified under ABC transporter complexes. MlaFEDB is an ABC transporter, so GO:0043190 ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter complex is the correct term.

The experiment robustly supports MlaB membership in the MlaFEDB ABC transporter complex, but GO:1990531 is defined as a P-type ATPase complex. Replace with GO:0043190 ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter complex.

MlaB itself performs the stabilization by binding the MlaF NBD. MlaF cannot be expressed and purified alone but is obtained in good yield when co-expressed with MlaB; without MlaB, MlaF does not stably associate with MlaE/MlaD; and MlaF over-expression bypasses the mlaB deletion, indicating that MlaF stabilization is the principal MlaB activity. Thong et al. independently found reduced MlaF levels without MlaB.

The MlaC-MlaD interaction is real and functionally central (it is the docking step for phospholipid exchange, later solved structurally in PMID:39080293), but generic protein binding conveys no function. The informative content is captured by the phospholipid transfer activity and phospholipid binding terms proposed below and by intermembrane phospholipid transfer. Removal follows the protein binding policy and does not question the interaction.

Correct but general. The transport MlaC performs is specifically the movement of phospholipid between the two envelope membranes through the periplasm, which is GO:0120010 intermembrane phospholipid transfer (an is_a descendant of phospholipid transport), already carried by MlaC via IBA and IDA. The cached paper is abstract-only, but UniProt cites it with experimental evidence for the mlaC disruption phenotype, and the refinement does not challenge the curator's claim.

Correct and at the right specificity; MlaC is targeted to the periplasm by a cleaved signal sequence and functions there. E. coli MlaC appearing in its own WITH/FROM reflects its experimental grounding.

Only the abstract is cached so the MlaC-specific fraction cannot be inspected, but a periplasmic assignment agrees with the signal peptide, the soluble periplasmic carrier role and the IBA row for the same term; deferring to the curator.
Correct but general: in a Gram-negative diderm bacterium the periplasm is the outer membrane-bounded periplasmic space, GO:0030288, which MlaC already carries (IBA, IDA; both ACCEPT).

MlaC carries out the aqueous-phase leg of the process: it receives phospholipid at one membrane complex and delivers it to the other, as shown by direct point-to-point transfer assays (PMID:34873038). The IBA node placement on the MlaC family is sound.

This 2017 paper demonstrates lipid occupancy and physical interactions with both membrane assemblies; its complete handoff is a model, not a measured transfer reaction. Independent later point-to-point transfer assays (PMID:34873038) establish the same biological process, so the process verdict remains ACCEPT without upgrading the original assay.

MlaC's molecular activity is not represented in GOA. GO:0120014 (removes a phospholipid from a membrane, transports it through the aqueous phase while protected in a hydrophobic pocket, delivers it to an acceptor membrane) matches MlaC exactly: lipid sits in a hydrophobic pocket (PMID:28388411), MlaC transfers to MlaFEDB (PMID:34873038), and MlaD transfers to MlaC (PMID:30284446). This is a molecular function directly demonstrated with purified protein, not an inference from necessity.

Direct structural evidence for phospholipid binding by E. coli MlaC; the binding state is the basis of its carrier activity and is reported independently by co-purification and apo/holo structures (PMID:31235958). Not redundant with GO:0120014, which is not an is_a descendant of phospholipid binding in GO.

Bare protein binding carries no functional information. The MlaD-MlaC interaction is a functionally important docking step for lipid hand-off, but it is better expressed through the phospholipid binding and phospholipid transfer activity annotations (and, at the model level, as MlaC input to the MlaFEDB activity) than by a generic binding term. Removal does not dispute the reported interaction.

Bare protein binding is uninformative. MlaD-MlaE contacts are subunit interfaces of the MlaFEDB ABC transporter, captured by the ABC transporter complex (GO:0043190) cellular component. Removal does not dispute the interaction.

Direct biochemical demonstration, independently confirmed by lipid co-purification with the MlaD periplasmic domain (PMID:28388411) and by a lipid acyl chain inserted into the MlaD pore in the MlaFEDB cryo-EM structure (PMID:33236984). Phospholipid binding is the defining molecular activity of MlaD.
MlaD is anchored in the inner membrane by an N-terminal signal-anchor helix and functions as part of the inner-membrane MlaFEDB complex; the native TM helix is required for assembly with MlaFEB.
Consistent with all subsequent biochemical and structural work placing MlaD in the inner-membrane MlaFEDB complex; accepted, deferring to the curator who read the full text.
Consistent with other structural work on the inner-membrane MlaFEDB complex; accepted, deferring to the curator.
Correct; the bacterial inner membrane is represented in GO by plasma membrane, and MlaD is a single-pass inner-membrane protein.

Correct but general. MlaD exchanges phospholipid with MlaC and channels it to/from the MlaE pocket as part of the Mla intermembrane transport system, i.e. GO:0120010 intermembrane phospholipid transfer (an is_a child of phospholipid transport), which is already annotated to this gene by IBA and IDA. GO:0120010 does not presuppose a net direction.
As for the IEA row: correct but general; the paper's own proposal is intermembrane phospholipid trafficking, which maps to GO:0120010.
MlaD is a membrane protein, but the term is too general; its established location is the inner (plasma) membrane, already annotated to the gene.

MlaD is a direct participant: its hexameric MCE ring binds phospholipid, forms part of the continuous lipid pathway with MlaE, docks MlaC and is required for MlaC-to-MlaFEDB lipid transfer. This is the core process.
Consistent with independent reconstitution data showing MlaD-dependent phospholipid transfer between MlaC and MlaFEDB; core process of MlaD.

MlaD binds phospholipid and purified MlaD donates lipid to MlaC (PMID:30284446); this is genuine transfer at the donor interface, not merely binding. It does not demonstrate all steps of the membrane-to-membrane carrier definition on MlaD itself. The reconstituted MlaFEDB/MlaC assay supports a contribution to this collective activity, retained in core_functions, rather than assigning the entire carrier activity to this individual subunit. This is a function-scope judgment, not a general rule that complex subunits must work in isolation.

Bare protein binding carries no functional information. The MlaE-MlaF and MlaE-MlaD contacts are subunit interfaces of the MlaFEDB complex, which is captured informatively by the ABC transporter complex (GO:0043190) cellular component. Removal does not dispute the reported interactions.

MlaE is a multi-pass integral inner-membrane protein whose topology was mapped experimentally and which functions in the inner-membrane MlaFEDB complex. In GO, the bacterial inner membrane is represented by plasma membrane.
The study analysed the E. coli K-12 inner-membrane proteome; MlaE inner-membrane location is consistent with all other evidence. Deferred to the curator who read the full data tables.
Consistent with topology mapping and structural work on the inner-membrane MlaFEDB complex; accepted, deferring to the curator who read the full text.
The UniProt location is experimentally supported (topology mapping), and plasma membrane is the GO term for the bacterial inner membrane.
MlaE is a multi-pass inner-membrane protein; the reporter-constrained topology model is the basis of UniProt's cytoplasmic/periplasmic domain assignments for MlaE.

Correct but general. MlaE moves phospholipid between the inner membrane and the periplasmic MlaD/MlaC lipid-binding sites as part of the Mla intermembrane transport system, which is precisely GO:0120010 intermembrane phospholipid transfer (an is_a child of phospholipid transport), a term already annotated to this gene. GO:0120010 does not encode direction; ATP-coupled retrograde transfer has direct reconstitution support, and the neutral ontology label does not imply equally established physiological directions.
As for the IBA row: correct but general. The paper itself proposes an intermembrane phospholipid trafficking role, which maps to the more specific GO:0120010 intermembrane phospholipid transfer.
MlaE is certainly a membrane protein, but the term is too general: its experimentally established location is the inner (plasma) membrane, a term already annotated to the gene.
MlaE is the transmembrane subunit of the MlaFEDB ABC transporter, shown biochemically (co-purification of a stable MlaF2E2D6B2 complex) and by cryo-EM. This is the appropriate complex term.

MlaE forms the substrate pocket and translocation pathway of MlaFEDB, and reconstituted transfer assays from independent groups show phospholipid exchange between MlaFEDB and MlaC. This is the core biological process of the gene.

GO:0120014 requires phospholipid removal from a membrane or particle, protection in a hydrophobic pocket during aqueous transport, and delivery to an acceptor membrane or particle. MlaE supplies the membrane-embedded lipid pocket and passage to MlaD; it is not the soluble carrier that shields cargo across the aqueous periplasm. The reconstituted MlaFEDB/MlaC assay supports a contribution to this collective activity, retained in core_functions, rather than assigning the entire carrier activity to this individual subunit. This is a function-scope judgment, not a general rule that complex subunits must work in isolation.

Complex membership is well supported, but GO:1990531 is defined as a complex that functions as a phospholipid-translocating P-type ATPase (the P4-ATPase flippase family). MlaFEDB is an ATP-binding cassette transporter, not a P-type ATPase, so the appropriate complex term is GO:0043190 ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter complex, already annotated to this gene.

Direct structural and in vivo crosslinking evidence that MlaE itself binds phospholipid substrate in its pocket, independently corroborated by the E. coli structure of Tang et al. This substrate-binding activity is not in GOA for MlaE. It is a molecular function of MlaE, not an inference from necessity.

Bare protein binding is uninformative under the protein-binding policy. The GroEL co-purification from a large-scale tagging screen most likely reflects MlaF being a chaperonin folding client rather than a functional activity of MlaF. Removal does not dispute that the interaction was observed.

Bare protein binding is uninformative under the protein-binding policy; the GroEL interaction from a proteome-wide pull-down is a generic chaperonin-client contact and does not describe an MlaF function. Removal does not dispute the observed interaction.

Bare protein binding is uninformative; the interactions with MlaB and MlaE are subunit contacts within the MlaFEDB complex, already represented by the complex membership term (GO:0043190).

Correct (InterPro ABC transporter-like domain; ADP is bound in the MlaFB crystal structure), but ATP binding is a step of the catalytic cycle and less informative than the core ATP hydrolysis activity.

Correct but general. MlaF has no transmembrane segment; it is part of the cytoplasmic MlaFB portion of MlaFEDB docked onto MlaE, so GO:0031234 extrinsic component of cytoplasmic side of plasma membrane (part_of plasma membrane) is the precise location.

Correct but general. The transported substrates are phospholipids moved between the two envelope membranes, captured by GO:0120010 intermembrane phospholipid transfer, which MlaF already carries (IBA, IDA).
Correct but general; the specific supported process is intermembrane phospholipid transfer (GO:0120010, is_a phospholipid transport), already on MlaF by IBA and IDA.
